statement: In adults who smoke and had not smoked for at least 2 hours, who were not using nicotine replacement or in a stop-smoking programme and were mostly not trying to quit, in 19 randomized trials pooled from their raw data (a systematic review searched to May 2011; 15 trials with 797 observations for strength of desire to smoke and 17 with 837 for desire to smoke; Haasova et al., 2013), a short bout of exercise, mostly moderate walking or cycling, compared with sitting quietly or a similar passive activity is associated with less desire to smoke rated right afterwards: about 2 points less on a 1-to-7 scale (strength of desire −1.91, 95% CI −2.59 to −1.22; desire to smoke −2.03, −2.60 to −1.46). The abstract calls these standardized mean differences, but the methods compute differences in scale points. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4 points (I² 92% to 94%), and the three trials that included isometric (muscle-tensing) exercise showed among the smallest effects. Craving was rated only once, immediately or 5 minutes after exercising, so how long the reduction lasts, and whether it helps people stop or stay stopped, were not studied. Participants knew whether they had exercised, the review did not assess the trials' risk of bias, and 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and its authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 19 small studies, people who had not smoked for a few hours rated their urge to smoke lower straight after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still, by about 2 points on a 7-point scale. Every study found the same direction, but the size varied a lot, and tensing muscles while sitting helped least. The urge was measured only minutes later, people knew whether they had exercised, and no study here checked whether exercise helps people stop smoking.
population: Adults who smoke, abstaining for at least 2 hours in laboratory studies, not using nicotine replacement or in a cessation programme, mostly not trying to quit
exposure: A single short bout of physical activity, mostly moderate walking or cycling (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Sitting quietly or another passive condition (listening, a video, a cognitive task, body scanning)
outcome: Self-rated strength of desire to smoke and desire to smoke (single 7-point items) immediately or 5 minutes after the bout, adjusted for the rating before
magnitude: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire −1.91 points (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 trials, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 trials, 837 observations, I² 92.0%. One-stage model: −1.89 and −2.03, with 95% of trials' true effects expected between −3.56 and −0.22 and between −3.45 and −0.62. Single trials −0.22 to −4.54.

evidence.extracted: Searches ended on 31 May 2011 and were limited to English-language papers from 2004 onwards; eligible trials were randomized crossover or parallel trials with at least 2 hours of abstinence before baseline; people in cessation programmes or using NRT were excluded.

evidence.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1
evidence.extracted: 19 randomized trials (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, the rest theses) with 10 to 84 participants each; bouts of 5 to 40 minutes, mostly moderate walking or cycling, against passive controls; craving rated immediately before and after the bout, or 5 minutes after it in three studies.

evidence.locator: Results › All eligible studies › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 30); Tables 2 and 3 (p. 32)
evidence.extracted: Strength of desire −1.91 (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations, I² 92.0%.

evidence.locator: Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis; Parallel arm studies; Studies investigating physical activity of moderate intensity; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: One-stage model −1.89 (−2.52 to −1.26) and −2.03 (−2.54 to −1.51), with 95% mid-ranges of −3.56 to −0.22 and −3.45 to −0.62; parallel trials only −1.78 and −2.27; moderate intensity only −2.20 and −2.14.

evidence.locator: Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 33-34); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 34) and last paragraph (p. 35)
evidence.extracted: Every study favoured exercise, from −0.22 to −4.54 points for strength of desire; the three studies that included isometric exercise had among the smallest effects, with intervals including zero in two of them for strength of desire (−0.55 and −0.22), and the largest effect came from the study with the highest baseline craving.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 26); Methods › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 28); Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (p. 32)
evidence.extracted: The abstract reports the pooled results as standardized mean differences, but the methods derive each effect as the difference between groups in post-intervention ratings adjusted for baseline, and the one-stage model reports a mean difference.

evidence.locator: Results › Literature search (p. 28); Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph (p. 30); Declarations of interest (p. 35); References 27-29 and 39-67 (pp. 36-37)
evidence.extracted: Titles were screened by the first author alone; quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); the review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and the authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; editors' count from the reference list and the text: 17 of the 19 included trials list at least one of the review's authors.

risk_of_bias.note: Participants could not be blinded to exercising and the outcome is a self-rating taken minutes later; the trials' risk of bias was not assessed; most trials are by the review's authors.

inconsistency.note: All trials favour exercise, but the size ranges from about 0.2 to 4.5 points (I² 92% to 94%), only partly explained by the kind of exercise.

indirectness.note: Worded for the population and timing studied (temporary abstinence, craving minutes after exercise); quitting is not claimed.

publication_bias.note: Unpublished theses were included and gave similar results; no small-study test; not downgraded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias −1 (unblinded self-rated outcome, no appraisal of the trials, trials mostly by the review's authors) and inconsistency −1 (a tenfold range in size) give low. Worded as an association because the size, and how much of it is exercise rather than expectation, are uncertain, although the design is randomized. Status replicated: 19 trials from several research groups point the same way; agreement with an earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Roberts et al., 2012) is not counted as independent because the trials overlap.
